title: Verbal red flags in real conversations
body_md:
## Listen for a request to give up control

A suspicious conversation is rarely identified by one magic phrase. A caller may be polite and grammatical; a genuine support agent may use words like “urgent” or “verification.” Instead, track what the speaker asks you to surrender: time to think, the ability to consult someone else, control of your device, an account code, or freedom to use an official channel. The UK NCSC says polished messages can fool even experts; errors in spelling are no longer a reliable test.

Several phrases deserve a deliberate stop. “Do not tell anyone” isolates you. “Stay on the line while you transfer” prevents independent checking. “I know your address and last four digits” turns ordinary or leaked data into a false identity proof. “Read the code I just sent” may allow access to your account. “Install remote support so I can fix this” hands over device control. FTC guidance describes unsolicited tech-support calls and remote-access requests as a scam pattern. A legitimate IT department may use remote tools after you initiate a verified support ticket, so the tool name alone is not a universal verdict; the unexpected request and absence of independent approval are the problem.

A move to another app is also contextual. Friends and real businesses sometimes change channels. But if the move hides a financial request from the platform’s records or your workplace process, ask why. An actual bank’s fraud team may need to discuss a card issue, yet you can call the bank through its own contact details and work through its real procedure. Do not recite a one-time code or share your screen because an inbound caller knows a detail about you.

Use a neutral exit rather than an argument: “I will contact the organization through the route I already use.” Then end the exchange. If the situation concerns a device you already gave remote access to, disconnect the session and use trusted support for recovery; do not keep following instructions from the same caller. If a code or password was shared, use the account provider’s verified recovery flow promptly. The point is not to label every awkward conversation a scam. It is to preserve a chance to verify before control changes hands.

widget_config.goal: Identify conversational moves that remove independent control and exit to a verified channel before sharing access, codes or money.
widget_config.today_action: Rehearse one exit sentence aloud and save the real support route for an account or device you use.
widget_config.scope: General conversational safety. NCSC guidance is UK-facing and FTC tech-support guidance is US-facing; workplace remote-support procedures vary by organization.

sources.title: UK NCSC — how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: UK public guidance, published 2021, reviewed 2022; cues and independent contact, not a diagnostic test.

sources.title: US FTC — tech support scams
sources.scope: US consumer guidance; unsolicited remote-access requests and trusted support paths.

sources.scope: US consumer alert (January 2026); call back using an existing card, statement, app or official site.

blocks.title: Synthetic: surprise “security technician”
blocks.situation: An unsolicited caller says your laptop is leaking data. They ask you to install remote-access software, keep the call secret, and read an account code during setup.
blocks.analysis: The combination removes independent control: device access, isolation and an account credential. End the call without installing or sharing. If you already granted access, disconnect and contact trusted IT or the device provider through an established route.

blocks.title: Synthetic: approved workplace support session
blocks.situation: You opened a ticket through the company portal. A technician responds inside the ticket, and you independently confirm the session ID with known IT staff before approving a time-limited remote session.
blocks.analysis: A remote tool can be legitimate in a verified support workflow. Keep control of the session, follow your organization’s policy, and stop if the technician requests unrelated banking details or codes. The tool name alone does not classify the interaction.

blocks.title: The support conversation
blocks.setup: Three separate fictional inbound support attempts test isolation, an unexpected code and remote access. Each next prompt resets to a new contact, so ending one call does not resume it.

steps.prompt: They mention the login error and say, “Please stay with me; the case will disappear if you hang up.” What do you do?

choices.text: Stay because the timing proves they see your case.
choices.consequence: You lose the chance to verify the caller’s identity.
choices.explanation: Coincidence or leaked account activity can be used as part of a story.

choices.text: Ask for a non-sensitive case description, end the call, and open the provider’s support route yourself.
choices.consequence: You preserve the problem but move authentication outside the call.
choices.explanation: A real case should be visible or confirmable through the provider’s normal channel.

steps.prompt: Separate new support call: a one-time code arrives on your phone, and the caller asks you to read it back. What now?

choices.text: Read it; support initiated the code.
choices.consequence: The code may authorize a login or recovery. If shared, contact the provider through its established route promptly to secure the account.
choices.explanation: Do not disclose a code generated by a request you did not initiate in a verified flow.

choices.text: Keep the code private and do not enter it into a page the caller supplied.
choices.consequence: You avoid handing over an authentication step.
choices.explanation: Check your account through its own app or support if concerned.

steps.prompt: Another separate unsolicited support caller offers remote software as an “easier fix.” What is the best response?

choices.text: Install it because a remote session is always standard support.
choices.consequence: You could surrender device control to an unverified caller.
choices.explanation: Remote support may be legitimate only within a confirmed, initiated process.

choices.text: Decline the inbound setup and, if needed, start a fresh ticket in the known support portal.
choices.consequence: Any future remote session can be approved under the real process.
choices.explanation: This does not rule out legitimate technical help; it changes who controls its start.

blocks.debrief: Debrief: each contact is a fresh snapshot, not the continuation of a call you ended. Isolation, codes and device control each deserve an independent check. If a code was already disclosed, use the provider’s verified account-recovery route promptly; replay to practise stopping before disclosure.

questions.prompt: A technician on a ticket you opened asks for an approved remote session. Is “remote access” alone proof of fraud?

choices.text: Yes; no legitimate team ever uses remote tools.
choices.explanation: Verified support teams can use them under policy.

choices.text: No; confirm the ticket and technician through your established process before approving.
choices.explanation: Correct: context and independent approval matter.

questions.prompt: An inbound caller quotes your address and asks for a one-time code. What matters most?

choices.text: Do not share the code; reach the service through its established route.
choices.explanation: Correct: knowing personal details is not identity proof.

choices.text: Share it because the address proves access to your account.
choices.explanation: The address could have come from many sources.

questions.prompt: A friend asks to continue chatting in another app, with no access or money request. What follows?

choices.text: The app switch itself proves deception.
Keep normal boundaries; assess any later sensitive request separately.
choices.explanation: Correct: a cue is not a verdict without the action and context.
